title: Audit Sampling - Statistical and Nonstatistical Methods
learning_objectives: Understand when sampling is appropriate in an audit
Distinguish between statistical and nonstatistical sampling
Know how to determine appropriate sample sizes
Understand sampling risk and nonsampling risk
Apply attribute sampling for tests of controls
Apply variables sampling for substantive testing
Evaluate sample results and draw conclusions

content.overview: Audit sampling involves applying audit procedures to less than 100% of items within a population to draw conclusions about the entire population. Because auditors cannot examine every transaction or balance due to time and cost constraints, sampling provides an efficient method to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. AU-C 530 and AS 2315 govern audit sampling. Two main approaches exist: statistical sampling (uses probability theory to mathematically measure sampling risk) and nonstatistical sampling (uses professional judgment without statistical calculations). Both can be effective when properly applied. Understanding sampling is critical for the CPA AUD exam as it underlies much of audit methodology.

fundamental_concepts.sampling_definition: Application of audit procedures to less than 100% of items within a population of audit relevance such that all sampling units have a chance of selection to provide a reasonable basis for conclusions about the entire population

appropriate_for: Tests of controls performed on sample basis
Substantive tests of details when population is large
When 100% examination is not cost-effective or necessary
not_appropriate_for: Very small populations (may be more efficient to test 100%)
Items that are individually significant (should test 100% of these)
Unusual or non-routine transactions requiring specific attention
When substantive analytical procedures alone provide sufficient evidence
High-risk items or fraud indicators (may need 100% testing)
when_sampling_is_appropriate.required_judgment: Decision to sample requires professional judgment based on risk, materiality, population characteristics, and audit efficiency

sampling_risk.definition: Risk that auditor's conclusion based on a sample may differ from conclusion if entire population were examined
sampling_risk.cause: The sample may not be representative of the population

risk_of_assessing_control_risk_too_low.description: Sample suggests controls are effective when they are not
risk_of_assessing_control_risk_too_low.consequence: Auditor relies on controls and reduces substantive testing, but controls are actually ineffective - may fail to detect material misstatements
risk_of_assessing_control_risk_too_low.how_controlled: Larger sample sizes, lower risk of incorrect acceptance

risk_of_assessing_control_risk_too_high.description: Sample suggests controls are ineffective when they actually work
risk_of_assessing_control_risk_too_high.consequence: Auditor performs more substantive testing than necessary - audit is less efficient but not ineffective
risk_of_assessing_control_risk_too_high.seriousness: Less serious - affects audit efficiency (cost) but not effectiveness
risk_of_assessing_control_risk_too_high.result: Usually detected through additional work or comparing to other evidence

risk_of_incorrect_acceptance.description: Sample suggests balance is not materially misstated when it is
risk_of_incorrect_acceptance.consequence: Auditor concludes balance is fairly stated but material misstatement exists - may issue inappropriate opinion
risk_of_incorrect_acceptance.relationship_to_detection_risk: This IS detection risk - the risk auditor fails to detect material misstatement
risk_of_incorrect_acceptance.how_controlled: Larger sample sizes, lower acceptable risk level

risk_of_incorrect_rejection.description: Sample suggests balance is materially misstated when it's not
risk_of_incorrect_rejection.seriousness: Less serious - affects efficiency, not effectiveness
risk_of_incorrect_rejection.result: Usually corrected when auditor performs additional procedures

sampling_risk.inverse_relationship_to_sample_size: Larger samples = lower sampling risk; smaller samples = higher sampling risk
sampling_risk.cannot_be_eliminated: Sampling risk exists whenever less than 100% of population is tested; can be reduced but not eliminated

nonsampling_risk.definition: Risk that auditor reaches erroneous conclusion for any reason NOT related to sample size
causes: Failing to recognize errors in sample items
Inadequate definitions of deviation or misstatement
nonsampling_risk.relationship_to_sample_size: NOT affected by sample size - exists even with 100% testing
how_controlled: Clear definition of what constitutes error or deviation
Adequate planning and understanding of objectives

statistical_sampling.definition: Sampling approach that uses probability theory to select sample items and mathematically measure sampling risk
characteristics: Random sample selection (every item has known probability of selection)
Mathematical calculation of sample size based on risk and precision
Objective evaluation of results using statistical formulas
Can quantify sampling risk (e.g., 'At 95% confidence, deviation rate is below X%')
advantages: Objective measurement of sampling risk
Scientifically designed sample sizes
Defensible in court or regulatory review
Can extrapolate results to population mathematically
Reduces auditor bias in selection
disadvantages: May calculate larger sample size than professional judgment would suggest

nonstatistical_sampling.definition: Sampling approach that relies on professional judgment to determine sample size, select items, and evaluate results
characteristics: Still must have rational basis and representative sample
advantages: Simpler and easier to apply
More flexible
No need for statistical formulas or software
Can be as effective as statistical if well-designed
Allows auditor to use experience and judgment
disadvantages: Relies heavily on auditor competence and judgment
Cannot statistically project errors to population

statistical_vs_nonstatistical_sampling.effectiveness: Both can provide sufficient appropriate evidence when properly designed and executed
statistical_vs_nonstatistical_sampling.auditor_choice: Auditor chooses approach based on cost-benefit, complexity, risk, and firm policy

attribute_sampling.description: Statistical sampling method used primarily for TESTS OF CONTROLS to estimate deviation rate in population
attribute_sampling.purpose: Determine whether control is operating effectively (deviation rate is acceptably low)
attribute_sampling.outcome: Estimate percentage of times control deviated from prescribed procedure

key_concepts.deviation: Any instance where control did not operate as designed
key_concepts.tolerable_deviation_rate: Maximum deviation rate auditor is willing to accept and still assess control risk at planned level (typically 5-10%)
key_concepts.expected_deviation_rate: Auditor's best estimate of actual deviation rate in population based on prior experience (typically 0-2%)
key_concepts.risk_of_assessing_control_risk_too_low: Acceptable risk that sample indicates control is effective when it's not (typically 5-10%)

factors_increasing_sample_size: Lower risk of assessing control risk too low (want more confidence)
Larger population (minimal effect once population exceeds ~5,000)
determining_sample_size.formula_approach: Use statistical tables or software based on confidence level, tolerable rate, and expected rate
determining_sample_size.typical_sample_sizes: Range from 25-100 items depending on factors above

sample_selection_methods.random_selection: Every item has equal chance of selection - use random number table or generator
sample_selection_methods.systematic_selection: Select every nth item (e.g., every 20th transaction) with random start
sample_selection_methods.monetary_unit_sampling: Select based on dollar value - each dollar has equal selection probability
sample_selection_methods.note: For statistical sampling, random or systematic selection required

evaluating_results.example: 3 deviations in sample of 50 = 6% sample deviation rate
evaluating_results.determine_upper_deviation_limit: Use statistical tables to find upper limit at desired confidence level

decision_rule.if_upper_limit_below_tolerable_rate: Control can be relied upon; assessed control risk can be low
decision_rule.if_upper_limit_exceeds_tolerable_rate: Control cannot be relied upon; increase substantive testing
decision_rule.if_close_to_tolerable_rate: Consider other evidence, may test additional items

qualitative_considerations: Whether deviations could cause material misstatements

exam_example.scenario: Auditor testing purchase approval control. Tolerable deviation rate = 6%, Risk of assessing CR too low = 5%, Expected deviation rate = 1%
exam_example.sample_size: Statistical table indicates sample of 78 items
exam_example.testing: Auditor tests 78 purchase orders for approval signatures
exam_example.results: Finds 2 purchase orders without proper approval
exam_example.conclusion: Upper limit (6.5%) exceeds tolerable rate (6%), so cannot rely on control at planned level. Must either: (1) test more items, (2) accept higher control risk and increase substantive testing, or (3) test compensating controls

variables_sampling.description: Sampling methods used for SUBSTANTIVE TESTING to estimate dollar amount of misstatement or account balance
variables_sampling.purpose: Determine whether account balance is materially misstated
variables_sampling.outcome: Estimate of total dollar misstatement in population or estimate of true account balance

monetary_unit_sampling_mus.description: Most common variables sampling for CPA exam - samples individual dollars, with items containing more dollars having higher selection probability
monetary_unit_sampling_mus.how_it_works: Define each dollar as sampling unit; larger dollar items more likely to be selected
advantages: Automatically stratifies sample - focuses on larger dollar items
Can use even if no misstatements are expected
Efficient for testing overstatements
Sample size does not depend on population variability
Easy to design and select sample
If no errors found, strong evidence balance is fairly stated
disadvantages: Less effective for understatements (small/zero balance items have low selection probability)
Treatment of errors can be complex
Not suitable if expecting many errors
Requires recorded balance to sample from

key_parameters.tolerable_misstatement: Maximum monetary misstatement auditor willing to accept (often = performance materiality)
key_parameters.expected_misstatement: Auditor's estimate of actual misstatement (based on prior years, analytics)
key_parameters.risk_of_incorrect_acceptance: Risk auditor concludes balance is fairly stated when it's materially misstated (typically 5-10%; related to detection risk)
key_parameters.population_book_value: Recorded amount of account being tested

monetary_unit_sampling_mus.reliability_factors: Based on risk level: 5% risk = 3.0, 10% risk = 2.3 (from tables)

example_calculation.given: Accounts receivable book value = $500,000; Tolerable misstatement = $25,000; Risk of incorrect acceptance = 5% (reliability factor = 3.0); Expected misstatement = $0
example_calculation.selection: Select every $8,333rd dollar; item containing that dollar is tested

evaluating_results.if_no_misstatements_found: Strong evidence; can conclude balance not materially misstated
evaluating_results.if_misstatements_found: Calculate projected misstatement using tainting percentages
evaluating_results.tainting: Misstatement amount ÷ recorded amount of sample item
evaluating_results.projection: Sum of (tainting % × sampling interval) for all errors
evaluating_results.decision: If projected + allowance for sampling risk ≤ tolerable misstatement, accept balance; otherwise, likely misstated

classical_variables_sampling.description: Uses normal distribution theory to estimate population value or misstatement
types: Mean-per-unit estimation - estimate average item value, multiply by population size
Difference estimation - estimate average misstatement, project to population
Ratio estimation - calculate ratio of audit to book value, apply to population
classical_variables_sampling.when_used: When testing for understatements, when many errors expected, or when MUS not suitable
characteristics: Sample size depends on population variability (standard deviation)
Requires pilot sample or prior data to estimate variability
Can handle both overstatements and understatements equally
classical_variables_sampling.exam_relevance: MUS is more commonly tested on CPA exam; classical variables less common but may appear

nonstatistical_variables_sampling.description: Using professional judgment to determine sample size, select items, and evaluate results for substantive tests
common_approach: Test all items over certain dollar threshold (e.g., all items > $50,000)
Select representative sample of remaining items using haphazard or judgmental selection
Project errors to population judgmentally (simple extrapolation)
nonstatistical_variables_sampling.sample_size_judgment: Consider materiality, risk, population size, and desired precision
nonstatistical_variables_sampling.evaluation: If errors found are close to materiality when projected, likely material misstatement exists

general_principles.inverse_relationship_to_risk: Higher acceptable risk → smaller sample; Lower acceptable risk → larger sample
general_principles.relationship_to_materiality: Higher materiality/tolerable misstatement → smaller sample; Lower materiality → larger sample
general_principles.relationship_to_expected_errors: More expected errors → larger sample; Fewer expected errors → smaller sample
general_principles.population_size_effect: Minimal effect once population exceeds ~5,000 items

factors_increasing_sample_size: Lower acceptable risk of incorrect acceptance/assessing CR too low
Lower tolerable misstatement or deviation rate
Higher expected misstatement or deviation rate
Less reliance on other controls or procedures
Higher assessed risk of material misstatement
Prior period misstatements or control failures
factors_decreasing_sample_size: Higher tolerable misstatement or deviation rate
Strong internal controls tested and reliable
practical_considerations: Very small populations may warrant 100% examination
Items individually significant should be tested 100%
Auditor judgment applied within statistical framework

random_selection.description: Every item in population has equal and known probability of selection
random_selection.disadvantages: May require numbered population, time-consuming without software

systematic_selection.description: Select every nth item after random start
process: Calculate sampling interval (population size ÷ sample size)
Select random starting point between 1 and interval
systematic_selection.example: Population 10,000, sample 100: interval = 100. Random start = 37. Select items 37, 137, 237, 337...
systematic_selection.acceptable_for: Statistical sampling if population not ordered in biased way
systematic_selection.risk: If population has cyclical pattern matching interval, may introduce bias

haphazard_selection.description: Selecting items without conscious bias, attempting to represent population
haphazard_selection.not_random: Not truly random - unconscious bias may exist
haphazard_selection.example: Selecting invoices from file without pattern, trying to get mix from throughout year
haphazard_selection.caution: Must avoid bias (e.g., selecting easy-to-reach items only)

block_selection.example: Select all transactions in March and September
block_selection.generally_not_recommended: High risk of bias if block not representative
block_selection.when_used: Very rarely; only when other methods impractical

judgmental_selection.description: Auditor selects specific items based on judgment
judgmental_selection.cannot_extrapolate: Cannot statistically project results to population

stratification.description: Dividing population into subgroups (strata) and sampling each separately
stratification.example: Divide A/R into: >$100K, $25K-$100K, <$25K; sample each stratum
advantages: More efficient - can test 100% of large items, sample small items
Reduces variability within strata
Smaller overall sample size may be needed
Focuses audit effort appropriately
stratification.common_approach: Test 100% of items above threshold, sample remaining items

project_errors_to_population.statistical_sampling: Use formulas to calculate most likely misstatement and upper/lower limits
project_errors_to_population.nonstatistical_sampling: Simple extrapolation: (Errors found ÷ sample $) × population $ = projected error
project_errors_to_population.example: Sample $100,000 of $1M population; found $2,000 errors. Projected = ($2,000 ÷ $100,000) × $1,000,000 = $20,000

compare_to_tolerable_misstatement.if_projected_much_less_than_tolerable: Evidence supports conclusion balance not materially misstated
compare_to_tolerable_misstatement.if_projected_exceeds_tolerable: Likely material misstatement; balance probably misstated

qualitative_evaluation: Nature and cause of errors (fraud vs. error)
Client's willingness to investigate and correct
actions_when_errors_found: Ask client to investigate and correct identified errors
Evaluate whether errors indicate greater problem
Consider impact on control risk assessment
If material misstatement likely, request adjustment or modify opinion
Document errors and projection in workpapers

anomalous_errors.definition: Error that is demonstrably not representative of population
anomalous_errors.example: One-time data entry error with specific identifiable cause
anomalous_errors.treatment: May exclude from projection IF auditor obtains high degree of certainty it's isolated
anomalous_errors.caution: Difficult to prove anomalous; use this exception rarely and document thoroughly

dual_purpose_testing.definition: Sample serves both as test of control AND substantive test
dual_purpose_testing.when_used: When same sample can efficiently accomplish both objectives
dual_purpose_testing.design: Design sample to meet more stringent of the two objectives (typically control testing requires larger sample)
dual_purpose_testing.evaluation: Evaluate separately for each purpose using appropriate criteria
dual_purpose_testing.efficiency: Can save time but must carefully design to achieve both objectives

key_concepts_to_memorize: Sampling risk: risk sample not representative; reduced by larger samples
Nonsampling risk: risk of human error; not affected by sample size
Type II error (incorrect acceptance/assessing CR too low) is MORE serious - affects effectiveness
Type I error (incorrect rejection/assessing CR too high) is LESS serious - affects efficiency
Attribute sampling for tests of controls (deviation rates)
Variables sampling (especially MUS) for substantive tests (dollar amounts)
Factors increasing sample size: lower risk, lower tolerable misstatement, higher expected errors
Statistical requires random selection; nonstatistical can use haphazard/judgmental
common_exam_questions: Which factor would increase/decrease sample size?
What is risk of incorrect acceptance vs. incorrect rejection?
When is attribute vs. variables sampling used?
How to calculate MUS sample size?
What does auditor do when sample results show likely misstatement?
Difference between statistical and nonstatistical sampling
Which selection method is appropriate for statistical sampling?

formulas.mus_sample_size: (Population Book Value × Reliability Factor) ÷ Tolerable Misstatement

tricks_to_remember: More serious errors: Type II errors (incorrect acceptance/assessing CR too low) - affects audit EFFECTIVENESS
Less serious errors: Type I errors (incorrect rejection/assessing CR too high) - affects audit EFFICIENCY only
Attribute = Controls (both start with consonants); Variables = Substantive (both start with vowels/s)
MUS = Monetary Unit = $ testing = Substantive tests
Random or systematic for statistical; haphazard OK for nonstatistical

summary: Audit sampling enables auditors to draw conclusions about populations by testing less than 100%. Two main types exist: attribute sampling (for testing controls, estimating deviation rates) and variables sampling (for substantive tests, estimating dollar misstatements). Within each, auditors choose statistical (objective, mathematical) or nonstatistical (judgment-based) approaches. Sample size is inversely related to risk and directly related to expected errors. Larger samples reduce sampling risk but cannot eliminate it entirely or address nonsampling risk. Monetary Unit Sampling (MUS) is the most tested variables method on the CPA exam. Key distinction: Type II errors (incorrect acceptance, assessing CR too low) are MORE serious as they affect audit effectiveness, while Type I errors affect only efficiency. Understanding when to use each method, how to determine sample sizes, and how to evaluate results is essential for AUD exam success.
